learningObjectives.title: Thinking and learning (conditioning, social learning, schemas, dual processing, biases)

questions.q: In classical conditioning (Pavlov), a dog salivates to a bell because the bell has been:
options: Repeatedly paired with food until it triggers the response
Reinforced with a reward for salivating
questions.explain: Classical conditioning pairs a neutral stimulus with an unconditioned stimulus until it elicits the response.

questions.q: Operant conditioning (Skinner) explains behaviour as shaped by:
questions.explain: Operant conditioning shapes behaviour through its consequences.

questions.q: Social (observational) learning was demonstrated by:
questions.explain: Bandura showed behaviour can be learned by observing and imitating models.

questions.q: Kahneman's dual-processing model contrasts:
options: Fast, automatic System 1 with slow, effortful System 2
questions.explain: System 1 is intuitive and fast; System 2 is deliberate and slow. Many biases stem from System 1.

questions.q: Schema theory (e.g. Bartlett) proposes that prior knowledge structures:
options: Guide how we interpret and remember information
questions.explain: Schemas shape interpretation and recall, which can cause reconstructive errors.

questions.q: Confirmation bias is the tendency to:
options: Favour information that supports existing beliefs
Remember the first list item best
Rely on the most recent information
questions.explain: Confirmation bias leads people to seek and interpret evidence that fits prior beliefs.

questions.q: A student only reads articles that agree with their view and dismisses the rest. This illustrates:
questions.explain: Selectively attending to belief-consistent evidence is confirmation bias, a System 1 tendency.

questions.q: 'Vicarious reinforcement' increases imitation when the model is:
questions.explain: Observing a rewarded model increases the likelihood of imitation.

questions.q: The working memory model (Baddeley & Hitch) handles verbal information in the:
questions.explain: The phonological loop processes speech-based information; the sketchpad handles visual/spatial material.

questions.q: The multi-store model distinguishes sensory memory, short-term memory and:
questions.explain: Atkinson and Shiffrin proposed three structurally separate stores.

questions.q: Loftus and Palmer's leading-question study ('smashed' vs 'hit') shows that memory is:
questions.explain: Question wording altered recall, showing memory is reconstructive and can be distorted.

questions.q: Because memory is reconstructive, eyewitness testimony should be treated as:
options: Potentially unreliable and open to distortion
questions.explain: Leading questions, misinformation and schemas can all distort eyewitness accounts.

questions.q: Perception is described as combining bottom-up sensory data with:
questions.explain: Perception is shaped by both incoming data and prior expectations/context.

questions.q: Selective attention is illustrated by the:
questions.explain: The cocktail-party effect shows we filter and focus on relevant information amid distraction.

questions.q: A strength of laboratory experiments in cognitive psychology is:
questions.explain: Lab control isolates the IV to support causal claims, though tasks can be artificial.

questions.q: A common weakness of laboratory memory experiments is:
questions.explain: Artificial tasks and settings may not reflect memory in everyday life.

questions.q: The 'Google effect' (Sparrow et al.) suggests people who expect information to be saved on a computer:
options: Remember where to find it rather than the information itself
questions.explain: People offload storage to devices (transactive memory), recalling location over content.

questions.q: Reaction time and accuracy are commonly used to:
questions.explain: Cognitive processes are inferred from objective performance measures such as reaction time and accuracy.

questions.q: A shopper judges a discounted price as good mainly because of the higher 'original' price shown. This reflects:
questions.explain: An initial reference value (anchor) biases subsequent judgement — an anchoring bias.

questions.q: The debate over whether language shapes thought concerns:
options: How far the language we use influences cognition
questions.explain: Psychologists debate the extent to which language structures or influences thought.
